The FOMC minutes released in early April, which caused some markets to take fright, referred to a meeting held before Dr Bernanke’s end-March call for faster US growth and contained details that merit a different interpretation. The commodities sector may therefore have over-reacted in the short term, but while uncertainty prevails there is little likelihood of a rebound in the near term._** **•** **_Physical support from East Asia helped to put a floor of $1,620 beneath gold during March, despite the Indian jewellers’ strike. This support is now receding in places and a further downward leg in price is expected during the second quarter, before an investor-led recovery develops in the second half of this year. We do not rule out QE3 and although we have modified our view from our previous One Year Forecast, we nevertheless believe that gold will surpass $1,900 before the end of 2012._** - **_Sliver found support at $31-$32 during March, but buying_** - **_was largely technical and there was little evidence of physical buying in the market with the exception of some early interest in India. Platinum will remain in surplus in 2012, although a small price premium over gold may be reestablished in the short term, aided by a shortfall in supply_** **_from Impala. North American auto sales figures are healthy, but scrap supplies continue to increase and it is likely that some auto producers are carrying inventory. Sales from the Russian State Depository are expected to be substantially reduced this year, laying the foundations for a renewed bull market. The minutes from the federal open market committee (fomc) that were released on 3rd April, and which caused some renewed consternation in the commodities markets (as well as boosting the dollar), referred to the meeting of 13th march. Press coverage of the minutes played up the potentially hawkish elements that they contained, such as the improvements in employment, manufacturing production and housing market activity, plus the increase in households’ real income. The minutes also noted, however, that conditions in residential mortgage markets generally remained depressed and that commercial real estate loans held by banks continued to decline. The “staff economic outlook” projected higher real GDP growth than previously “justly reflecting an improved outlook for economic activity abroad, a lower foreign exchange value for the dollar and a higher projected part of equity prices....[but] that real GDP growth would pickup only gradually in 2012 and 2013, supported by accommodative monetary policy, easing credit conditions and improvements in consumer and business sentiment”. The fomc also suggested that the unemployment rate would decline gradually towards levels that the committee judges to be consistent with its dual mandate. Here lies the conundrum that suggests that the markets may have over-reacted to the downside when the minutes were released.
